# Diagnosing High-Pitched Scratching on Cold Starts in Older Ford Bantams

A high-pitched screech immediately upon turning the key, which persists briefly after the ignition is cut off, points directly to a mechanical bind or insufficient lubrication within the starting circuit. In your specific case with the 1980s-era Ford Bantam 1.3L, this symptom usually isolates the starter motor or its engagement mechanism rather than an accessory like an idler pulley. The fact that the noise continues for a fraction of a second after you release the key is particularly telling; it indicates the starter solenoid is holding the drive gear (Bendix) against the flywheel even when power is removed, suggesting the pinion gear never fully retracted or is rubbing against the ring gear teeth.

The secondary symptom—a high idle that drops and requires throttle input before stabilizing—is a classic sign of an irregular combustion event at startup. When the starter motor struggles to reach full cranking speed due to internal drag or poor engagement, it may "lug" the engine or fail to build sufficient cylinder pressure quickly enough. This can cause one or more cylinders to miss their power stroke initially, triggering the Engine Management System (if equipped) or the mechanical governor to adjust idle air volume aggressively before settling into a normal rhythm once the starter disengages and the ECU regains control of the throttle body.

Given that your vehicle recently underwent a general service, it is highly probable the issue lies within components not covered by standard belt changes or fluid flushes. The most likely culprit is the starter motor itself. In older Ford engines, these units often suffer from worn carbon brushes or a failing solenoid plunger. If the internal springs are fatigued, they may not return the pinion gear to its resting position fast enough after cranking stops, resulting in that post-cut-off screech.

You can verify this without immediately replacing the part by performing a manual engagement test. Locate the small button on the starter solenoid housing (usually near the battery cable connection). With the ignition key off, press and hold this button manually while simultaneously turning the key to the "Start" position for only two seconds. If the engine cranks normally without noise, the issue is likely a sticky internal mechanism or worn teeth on the starter pinion that require cleaning or part replacement.

Another possibility involves the flywheel ring gear. Over 31,000 kilometers in harsh South African driving conditions could have led to localized wear on specific teeth of the ring gear. If a single tooth is broken or heavily worn, the starter pinion will scrape against it repeatedly until it skips over the damaged spot, creating that distinct metallic screech followed by successful engagement.

Before condemning the starter, inspect the battery terminals for corrosion and ensure the ground strap connecting the chassis to the engine block is clean and tight. A weak voltage drop during cranking can cause the solenoid to chatter or engage partially, mimicking these symptoms. However, given the persistence of the noise after key release, a replacement starter assembly is often the most cost-effective and reliable solution for this specific model year.

If you decide to proceed with diagnostics, ensure you have a multimeter capable of measuring voltage under load. Check for 12 volts at the main power terminal on the solenoid while cranking. If voltage is present but the starter does not engage fully, the issue is mechanical rather than electrical. Replacing the unit typically resolves both the noise and the erratic idle behavior, as a fresh motor provides consistent torque from zero RPM.
